title: An early portable computer weighed about 11 kg
body: The Osborne 1 went on sale in 1981. At about 11 kg, it packed a 13 cm display, two floppy drives and a keyboard into a case people could take from one desk to another.
takeaway: Portable once meant you could carry the whole setup, even if you needed a table to use it.
source: Computer History Museum, Timeline of Computer History (1981)
visual: an open suitcase-style early computer with a small blank display

title: A 1972 home games console ran without stored software
body: The Magnavox Odyssey connected to a television and could play several games, including a form of table tennis. It used electronic circuitry to make the screen images without a microprocessor or stored software.
takeaway: The same kind of screen play can be built with dedicated circuits or with instructions for a general-purpose chip.
source: Computer History Museum, Playing at Home
visual: an unbranded early games console next to a television with simple dots of light

title: The basic Altair computer took input through toggle switches
body: The Altair 8800, introduced in 1975, had front-panel switches and lights in its basic configuration. A user could set bits with the switches and read values back from patterns of lights.
takeaway: A keyboard and screen make the machine's electrical state easier to work with, but neither is essential for computing.
source: Computer History Museum, Altair 8800 Front Panel
visual: a vintage computer front panel with a row of small switches and lamps
